title: Oankar made all
hook: from the One came Brahma and all creation

segments.voice: Yesterday, an alphabet of wisdom: Oankar, Guru Nanak's poem on the letters. Your line was letters of wisdom. Which word did you choose on purpose? Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

Pick up the nearest object. A mug, say. Someone shaped it, someone fired it, someone dug the clay. The clay came out of a hillside, and the hillside came out of something older still. Keep following any made thing back, and the trail gets long and strange very fast. The Oankar starts at the far end of that trail. Its opening lines don't begin with a letter to learn. They begin with where everything came from. Today: Oankar made all.
screen: `A MUG, A POTTER, A HILLSIDE.` → `FOLLOW IT BACK.` → `THE OANKAR STARTS AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Here is the opening of the Oankar, in paraphrase. From Oankar, Brahma came to be. Brahma kept Oankar in his mind. From Oankar came the mountains and the ages. From Oankar the Vedas were made. Remember who Nanak is speaking to, in the tradition: a pandit, a teacher of the Vedas. So the poem opens in the pandit's own world. Brahma, the creator in the pandit's own tradition. The Vedas, the scriptures he taught. Nanak doesn't dismiss any of them. He traces each one back to its source. Brahma came from the One, and remembered the One. The mountains, the long ages of time, the holy books themselves: from Oankar. It's the same move we watched in the Sidh Gosht, using the other person's language, now in a schoolroom instead of on a mountain. And it's the move the mug made a minute ago. Whatever is in front of you, a scripture, a mountain, a cup, follow it back far enough and the poem says you arrive at one place. Notice the word kept in that second line. Brahma kept Oankar in his mind. In the poem, even Brahma, the creator, is a rememberer. That matters for an ordinary day. If everything comes from the One, then nothing in front of you is a stranger to it. That's a week's worth of lines, really. The Name in the breath. Yoga in daily life. The yogis bowed. Answer kindly. Keep talking. Letters of wisdom. And now, the root under all of them: from the one.
screen: `FROM OANKAR, BRAHMA.` · `THE MOUNTAINS, THE AGES, THE VEDAS.` · `THE PANDIT'S OWN WORLD, TRACED BACK.` · `NOTHING IS A STRANGER TO IT.` · then, large: `FROM THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one made thing. Choose something within reach: a cup, a pencil, a shoe, a slice of bread. Hold it or rest your eyes on it. Then follow it back one step at a time. Who made it. What it was made of. Where that came from. And before that. Go slowly. Don't hurry to an answer at the end. Just keep stepping back, and notice how many hands and how much earth are in one small thing. If you pray, you can let the trail end in the One the Oankar names. If you don't, rest in the wonder of the trail itself. The bell holds the time.
Oankar made all. The poem's opening: from Oankar came Brahma, the mountains, the ages and the Vedas. Today's word.
Your line: from the one. Today, pick one thing you use without thinking, your keys, your phone, your lunch, and trace it back three steps before you use it. Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: The Guru Granth Sahib opens with Ik Oankar, the One Creator; the Oankar in Raga Ramkali opens by tracing all creation back to that One.

fork.setup: you're answering a pandit who teaches the Vedas. how does the Oankar open?
options: by saying the Vedas are wrong.
by tracing Brahma, the mountains and the Vedas back to the One.
by leaving his scriptures out entirely.
fork.reveal: from Oankar, Brahma; from Oankar, the mountains and the ages; from Oankar, the Vedas. the poem meets him in his own world.

original.note: Oankar: a name for the One, and the word each of the poem's opening lines begins with.

notes: Opening of the Oankar paraphrased: from Oankar Brahma was born; Brahma kept Oankar in his consciousness; from Oankar the mountains and ages came; from Oankar the Vedas were made. Please confirm paraphrase and Ang 929.

Brahma is described as 'the creator in the stories the pandit knew'; the script is careful not to dismiss Hindu tradition. Please check that the framing is respectful to Hindu listeners and accurate to the hymn.
Trapdoor and original: the opening lines are said to begin with ਓਅੰਕਾਰਿ / ਓਅੰਕਾਰੁ; please confirm.
Week end (days 1142–1148): the teach closes by naming the week's lines.
howItsDone: the Guru Granth Sahib opens with Ik Oankar (Mool Mantar); please confirm the gloss One Creator.

Editor: replaced 'the creator in the stories the pandit knew', 'a god in a story' and 'the great creator in the story' with wording that doesn't frame Hindu tradition as stories: 'the creator in the pandit's own tradition' and 'in the poem, even Brahma, the creator, is a rememberer'.
